title: Your Boss Is Solving a Different Problem Than You Are
author: leadwithkelly
summary: The Lead With Kelly newsletter explores the systematic misunderstanding that occurs when employees assume their manager is working on the same problem they are. The piece argues that managers operate in a fundamentally different problem space: while employees are solving for task completion, quality, and immediate outcomes, managers are simultaneously managing board expectations, absorbing the fallout of failed organizational bets, protecting their own standing in internal political dynamics, and maintaining enough credibility to advocate for their teams in rooms their teams never see. The piece does not ask employees to feel sorry for their managers; it asks them to develop the interpretive sophistication to understand why their manager's behavior often seems inexplicable when viewed only from the employee's problem space. The key practical implication is that employees who learn to model their manager's problem space -- to ask 'what is she actually trying to solve for right now?' -- become dramatically more effective at getting what they need and at contributing what actually matters.
points: * Managers operate in a fundamentally different problem space from employees: while employees are solving for task completion and immediate quality, managers are simultaneously managing board expectations, failed bets, internal standing, and absent-room advocacy. * Most employee-manager miscommunication stems not from bad intentions on either side but from each party assuming the other is working on the same problem -- they are not. * The employee who learns to model their manager's actual problem space -- asking 'what is she solving for right now?' rather than 'why isn't she focused on my thing?' -- becomes dramatically more effective at both getting what they need and contributing what actually matters. * The piece identifies a specific failure mode in high-performing employees: they are excellent at their own problem space and assume that excellence is sufficient, not realizing that their manager's approval requires solving a different problem entirely. * Organizational effectiveness requires bidirectional translation: managers should be explicit about their problem space and constraints, and employees should develop the interpretive habit of asking what problem the manager is actually holding.
quotes: Your boss is not solving the problem you are solving. She is solving the problem she is in. Those two problems overlap -- sometimes significantly -- but they are not the same problem, and acting as if they are is one of the most reliable sources of mutual frustration in organizational life.

When she doesn't prioritize the thing that seems obviously important from where you sit, it is usually not because she is incompetent or careless. It is because, from where she sits, she is holding three other problems that you cannot see: the board conversation that went sideways last quarter, the project that was a big bet and didn't land, the colleague who is advocating loudly for a different direction in the rooms you're not in.

The employees who get the best outcomes are the ones who have developed a theory of their manager's problem space. Not a cynical theory -- a genuinely curious one. What does she care about most right now? What is she most worried about? What would make her look good to the people she reports to? These are not manipulative questions. They are interpretive ones.

High-performing employees often hit a ceiling not because their work quality drops but because they stop solving for their manager's problem. They assume their output quality is self-explanatory. It rarely is. Output that doesn't connect to what your manager is actually trying to accomplish -- however good it is -- is output that will be invisible.

The most effective thing you can do this week is have a conversation with your manager that starts with: 'I want to understand what problem you're most focused on solving right now.' That question will change the quality of every conversation you have with her afterward.
